messages.subject: Re: Retrieving contexts
messages.body_plain:
Eloiz, one simplistic way to get more surrounding context is to
collapse the corpus file into a single vector before running
exact.matches:

corpus.file<-scan("/Users/brow2662/Desktop/Chiara08_utf8.txt",
what="char", sep="\n")

corpus.file<-paste(corpus.file, collapse=" ")

hits<-exact.matches(search.expression, corpus.file)[[4]]

This would give you an over load of surrounding context as it would
give you the entire corpus file as the surrounding context for each
match. You could eliminate the excess in a spreadsheet with "right"
and "left" functions. You could also eliminate the excess in R by
adding an argument to exact.matches that delimits the amount of
surrounding context to be pulled around each match.

Best of luck, Earl Brown

messages.subject: Computing keyness
messages.body_plain:
How exactly is 'keyness' measured? To be clear: I'm not asking how to do it in R; I'm asking how to do it period.

So you need two corpora. One is presumably general purpose and the other is a collection of texts (or just one text) in a specific genre or topic. You do a word frequency analysis of both, and in the process you identify words in the narrow corpus that are much higher than in the general one. So far this is easy. But how is a keyness score assigned? I'm helping a colleague with some data he analysed with Wordsmith. When run through the Keyword tool, you get a keyness score as well as a P(robability) score. (See bottom graphic at: http://www.lancs.ac.uk/fss/courses/ling/corpus/blue/l03_2.htm )

By what formulae are the keyness and P actually calculated? Can anyone help me out here?

--
Kevin Parent, Ph.D, ACS, ALB
Korea Maritime University
Chair, Korea Toastmasters Territorial Council

National Korea Toastmasters: www.koreatm.org <http://www.koreatm.org>

Hi Kevin,

It’s either a chi-square or (more often) a log-likelihood score, from which the p-value is then deduced relative to the critical values for the chi-square distribution. You can find the formula for LL plus lots of refs here: http://ucrel.lancs.ac.uk/llwizard

(Incidentally I was responsible, in my wayward youth, for putting up that website you cite based on a colleague’s course notes. Ouch! blue links on blue background! What can I say, I didn’t really know much HTML back then...)

best

Andrew.

messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Computing keyness
messages.body_plain:
? How exactly is 'keyness' measured? To be clear: I'm not asking how

to do it in R; I'm asking how to do it period.

That would then be more of a general corpora question (plus the answer
is already in the answer key to the semantics 3 assignment on the
companion website) but to make it legit for this list, let me answer
this way ;-)

########################
# I am using another measure that I like better because of its
simplicity, the relative frequency ratio, the script is inelegant
(using a loop)
# generate random corpora
set.seed(1)
corpus <- sample(letters[1:10], 100, replace=TRUE)
reference.corpus <- sample(letters[2:11], 1000, replace=TRUE)

# generate frequency lists (percentages)
corpus.freqlist <- prop.table(table(corpus))
reference.corpus.freqlist <- prop.table(table(reference.corpus))

# structure to collect keywords and their values
keywords.for.corpus <- vector(length=length(corpus.freqlist))
names(keywords.for.corpus) <- names(corpus.freqlist)

# do the work
# the ifelse with the "min(reference.corpus.freqlist)/10" deals with
words that do not show up in the reference corpus
# by for them dividing by 1/5 of the smallest observed frequency in
the reference corpus
for (word in names(corpus.freqlist)) {
   keywords.for.corpus[word] <- corpus.freqlist[word] / ifelse
(is.na <http://is.na>(reference.corpus.freqlist[word]),
min(reference.corpus.freqlist)/5, reference.corpus.freqlist[word])
}

# words that are key/distinctive for corpus and logging it gives a
nice scale centered around 0
sort(keywords.for.corpus, decreasing=TRUE)
qwe <- log(sort(keywords.for.corpus, decreasing=TRUE))
plot(qwe, type="h", ylim=c(1.1*range(qwe)), xlab="",
ylab=expression(paste(log[nat], " rel. freq. ratio (key for
corpus)")))
   grid(); abline(h=0); text(seq(qwe), qwe, names(qwe),
pos=ifelse(qwe>0, 3, 1), font=3)
########################

Cheers,
STG
--
Stefan Th. Gries
-----------------------------------------------
University of California, Santa Barbara
http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries
-----------------------------------------------

messages.subject: New character-processing function(ality) 1
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

I am not sure how much you all are following R development and
updating your R versions regularly, but today's update is something
you should update, too: in addition to increases in speed, there are
several text processing changes that should be very useful:

- regexpr() and gregexpr() with perl = TRUE allows Python-style named captures.
- agrep() gains a fixed argument to optionally allow approximate
regular expression matching, and a costs argument to specify possibly
different integer match costs for insertions, deletions and
substitutions.
- new function regexec() for finding the positions of matches as well
as all substrings corresponding to parenthesized subexpressions of the
given regular expression.
- new function aregexec() in package utils for finding the positions
of approximate string matches as well as all substrings corresponding
to parenthesized subexpressions of the given regular expression.

Cheers,
STG
--
Stefan Th. Gries
-----------------------------------------------
University of California, Santa Barbara
http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries
-----------------------------------------------

messages.subject: New character-processing function(ality) 2
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

This is let you know that I have revised exact.matches a bit. You can
get the new version by sourcing from
<http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries/exact_matches.r>. The
main two changes can be inferred from formals:

###################
$search.expression

$corpus.vector

$pcre
[1] TRUE

$case.sens
[1] TRUE

$characters.around
[1] 0

$lines.around
[1] 0

###################

That is,

- there is a new argument characters.around where you can specify the
number of characters around the match you want;
- there is a new argument lines.around where you can specify the
number of corpus lines around the match you want.
(One of the two must be 0 or left alone.)

Testing so far indicates it works (thanks to Earl Brown for some
comments/feedback), but I can of course not offer any guarantees: as
always, use at your own risk. (Any bug reports or other comments would
of course be much appreciated and acknowledged.)

Cheers,
STG
--
Stefan Th. Gries
-----------------------------------------------
University of California, Santa Barbara
http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries
-----------------------------------------------

messages.subject: csv problem: very basic, really unnerving...
messages.subject_clean: csv problem: very basic, really unnerving...
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
I've got a strange problem reading csv files into R. With one of my
files, for instance, line 1 and 2 appear correctly in R, then the next
400 lines of the csv file inexplicably end up in line 3 of the
dataframe (in a complete mess!), and the rest of the table, from line
404 to 1000, looks fine. It seems as for these 400 lines, R skips all
tabstops and/or newline characters.

The csv files aren't exactly huge, they have about 1000 lines and
25-30 columns each. I use LibreOffice on MacOS X for coding and export
the tables as tab-delimited csv files, it's all by the book. I can't
remember having such problems on my old MacBook, it all began when I
first started using a new MacBook Pro about four weeks ago.

I've noticed that the problem doesn't occur when I delete the column
which contains the lines taken directly from the corpus. So I suspect
the problem may have to do with the txt encoding of the ICE corpora.
Interestingly, only files created from ICE-GB cause the problem, files
from ICE-SING don't. I've spent many hours trying to find some kind of
workaround: Re-saving the file with various text editors, different
encodings (Unicode, ASCII, Mac OS, Windows...), LF, CR, CR & LF as
newline characters, and I've scoured many R forums, but so far to no
avail.

Thank you in advance!

Thomas

messages.subject_clean: [CorpLing with R] csv problem: very basic, really unnerving...
messages.body_plain:
I bet this is due to (single and/or double) quotes in the corpus files
or other (sometimes hidden) characters. I just had a similar case
where a concordance I was sent first looked fine but upon import with
read.table threw cells out of alignment. You need to make sure that
you read in with read.table and that quote and comment.char are set to
"" and that there are no other encoding issues; this is how this
always worked out for me.

Cheers,
STG
--
Stefan Th. Gries
-----------------------------------------------
University of California, Santa Barbara
http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries
-----------------------------------------------

messages.subject: Break point for segemented regression
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Piecewise (or segmented) linear regression can be a useful alternative to simple linear regression; it fits different linear models to different segments of the explanatory variable x. The problem is to establish precisely where to set the break.

Is anybody aware of a simple method to determine that point?

Best
Chris
